prompt: Why is driving at night more dangerous than driving during the day?
choices: You cannot see as far ahead or as well to the sides
Speed limits are higher at night
Traffic signals work differently at night
Roads are much more crowded at night than in the daytime
explanation: At night your headlights limit how far you can see, and your ability to judge distances, see colors and use side vision is reduced. More tired and impaired drivers are also on the road.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 43-44, NY p. 62)

prompt: The headlights of an oncoming vehicle are blinding you. Where should you look?
choices: Directly at the oncoming headlights
Toward the right edge of the road
At the center line next to the oncoming car
Down at your dashboard until the car passes
explanation: Looking toward the right edge of the road keeps you from being blinded while still letting you stay on course. Watch the oncoming vehicle out of the corner of your eye.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 65, NY p. 63, TX p. 53)

prompt: An oncoming driver keeps their high beams on as they approach you at night. What is the best response?
choices: Switch on your high beams until the other driver dims theirs
Keep your low beams on and look to the right edge
Speed up so you pass them sooner
Stop in your lane until they go by
explanation: Do not "punish" the other driver by turning on your own high beams; that only blinds both of you. Stay on low beams, look to the right edge, and keep going at a safe speed.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 65, PA p. 44)

prompt: When should you switch from high beams to low beams?
choices: When you are approaching an oncoming vehicle
Only when the other driver flashes their lights at you
Only after you enter a city or town
Whenever you are on a dark, empty country road
explanation: High beams can blind oncoming drivers, so dim them when a vehicle approaches. The exact distance is set by state law; check your state's rule in the State Cheat Sheet.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 17, TX p. 53, NY p. 63)

prompt: You are using high beams and come up behind another vehicle traveling in your direction. What should you do?
choices: Keep high beams on so the driver knows you are there
Flash your high beams to ask the driver to speed up
Turn off your headlights and use parking lights
Switch to low beams so you don't blind the driver
explanation: Your high beams reflect in the mirrors of the vehicle ahead and can blind its driver. Dim your lights when following another vehicle; the exact distance varies by state.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 17, TX p. 53, NY p. 63)

prompt: Where are high-beam headlights most useful?
choices: In fog
In heavy rain or snow, to see farther ahead
On dark, open roads with no one nearby
On brightly lit city streets
explanation: High beams let you see farther on dark, open roads when no one is coming toward you or ahead of you. In fog, rain or snow they reflect back and reduce visibility.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 65, TX p. 53)

prompt: At night, the headlights of the car behind you reflect brightly in your inside rearview mirror. What can you do?
choices: Switch your own headlights to high beam
Turn on your interior dome light
Switch the mirror to its night setting
Turn on your rear window defroster
explanation: Most inside mirrors have a day/night setting that reduces glare from the headlights of following vehicles.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 44, NY p. 63)

prompt: At night, a vehicle with only one headlight is coming toward you. What should you keep in mind?
choices: It must be a motorcycle, so it will stay at the far edge of its own lane
It may be a motorcycle or a car with one light out, so keep right
One light means the vehicle is still far away
It is a bicycle, so you can stay near the center line
explanation: A single light could be a bicycle, a motorcycle or a car missing a headlight, and you cannot tell how wide it is. Keep as far to the right as is safe until it passes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 65, FL p. 81)

prompt: Which of these is usually hardest to see at night?
choices: A pedestrian wearing dark clothing
A car with its headlights on
A road sign with reflective lettering
A truck with lit marker lights
explanation: Pedestrians are harder to see at night than signs and other roadside objects, especially in dark clothing. Watch closely for them, along with bicyclists and motorcyclists.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 44, CA p. 65)

prompt: You pull out of a brightly lit gas station onto a dark road. What should you do?
choices: Drive at normal speed, since eyes adjust instantly
Use high beams even when other cars approach
Look at oncoming headlights to help your eyes adjust
Drive slowly until your eyes adjust to the dark
explanation: Your eyes need time to adjust after leaving a brightly lit area. Drive slowly until you can see well in the darkness.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 65)

prompt: Before a night drive, why should you clean your windshield and headlights?
choices: Dirt only matters for daytime driving
Dirty lenses can keep your headlights from switching on
Clean headlights are needed only when using high beams
Dirt adds glare and cuts the light from your headlights
explanation: A dirty windshield increases glare from oncoming headlights, and dirty headlights can give only a fraction of their normal light.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 63, PA p. 44)

prompt: In the late afternoon, when should you turn on your headlights?
choices: Only once it is completely dark
Only after the streetlights come on
As soon as daylight begins to fade
Only if another driver flashes their lights at you
explanation: Turning on headlights early helps other drivers and pedestrians see you. Your state also sets a legal time for headlight use; check your state's rule in the State Cheat Sheet.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 57, NY p. 63)

prompt: Why are dawn and dusk especially risky times to drive?
choices: Roads are always icy at those times
Light is poor and animals are most active
Traffic signals switch to flashing mode during those hours
Speed limits are automatically lowered
explanation: Visibility is poor in twilight, vehicles without headlights are hard to see, and deer and other animals move the most at dawn and dusk.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 64-65, FL p. 79, PA p. 43)

prompt: It is getting dark and your car's daytime running lights are on. Is that enough?
choices: No. Turn on your headlights so your taillights are lit too
Yes. Daytime running lights also light up the rear of the car
Yes, as long as your dashboard lights are on
No. Switch to parking lights instead
explanation: Daytime running lights usually do not turn on your taillights, so drivers behind you may not see you. Use your headlights; parking lights are not a substitute.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 44, NY p. 63)

prompt: You are driving into a low, bright sun in the early morning. What helps reduce glare?
choices: Use your sun visor and wear sunglasses
Turn on your high beams
Speed up to get through the glare quickly
Turn on your windshield wipers
explanation: Sun visors, sunglasses and a clean windshield all reduce glare. Slow down if glare makes it hard to see.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 66, AZ p. 54)

prompt: At sunset, the low sun is behind you as you drive. What should you be aware of?
choices: You have no glare risk, so you can follow more closely
Glare only affects drivers going your direction
Drivers behind you are blinded, so tap your brakes often
Oncoming drivers face the glare and may not see you
explanation: When the sun is behind you, drivers coming toward you are looking into it. They may not see your vehicle or turn signals, so drive with extra caution.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 54)

prompt: When is a paved road often the most slippery during a rainstorm?
choices: After it has rained steadily for several hours
Right after the rain stops
In the first few minutes after the rain begins
Only when it rains at night
explanation: When rain starts, it mixes with oil and grime on the pavement and makes a slick film. As rain continues, much of that oil washes away.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 44-45, CA p. 67, AZ p. 55)

prompt: What is hydroplaning?
choices: When your brakes overheat on a long downhill
When your tires ride on water instead of the road
When your engine stalls after a deep puddle
When fog forms on the inside of your windshield in the rain
explanation: In hydroplaning, water builds up under the tires faster than they can push it away, so the tires lose contact with the pavement and you can lose steering and braking control.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 68, PA p. 45, NY p. 63)

prompt: Your car starts to hydroplane on a wet highway. What should you do first?
choices: Ease off the gas and hold the wheel steady
Brake hard so the car stops as quickly as possible
Steer sharply toward the shoulder
Accelerate to push through the water
explanation: Let the car slow down gradually so the tires can regain contact with the road. Avoid hard braking and sudden steering, which can cause a skid.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 68, AZ p. 56, PA p. 45)

prompt: On a rainy road you hear a sloshing sound from your tires. What does it suggest?
choices: Your tires are low on air, so speed up to warm them
The road is draining well and grip is normal
Your windshield wipers need to be replaced
Enough water to risk hydroplaning, so slow down
explanation: Sloshing tires mean you are driving through a lot of water. Slow down to keep your tires in contact with the road.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 68)

prompt: How can you lower your risk of hydroplaning in heavy rain?
choices: Drive through puddles quickly so you spend less time in the water
Lower your tire pressure for better grip
Slow down and steer around standing water when you safely can
Turn on cruise control to avoid speed changes
explanation: Slowing down is the best way to prevent hydroplaning. Avoid standing water when it is safe to do so, and keep good tread and proper tire pressure.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 68, NY p. 63, AZ p. 55)

prompt: Why should you avoid using cruise control on wet, icy or snowy roads?
choices: Cruise control stops working when the temperature drops below freezing
It makes your headlights dim
Cruise control can keep giving power if the wheels slip
It is designed only for city driving
explanation: On a slippery road you need to reduce power to stop wheel spin and stay in control. Cruise control keeps feeding power and can make a skid worse.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 45, CA p. 69)

prompt: In a heavy downpour you can barely see the road ahead. What is the safest choice?
choices: Follow closely behind the taillights of the car ahead
Slow down, and pull off the road if you still can't see
Switch to high beams to see through the rain
Stop in your travel lane and wait
explanation: In very heavy rain you may see only a short distance ahead. Slow down; if conditions are too bad to drive, get fully off the road where you won't be hit.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 68, PA p. 46)

prompt: After driving through deep water, your brakes feel weak and pull to one side. What should you do?
choices: Drive slowly and brake lightly until the brakes dry
Pump the brakes hard at highway speed
Keep driving normally, since the brakes will dry on their own
Use only the parking brake until you get home
explanation: Wet brakes may not hold or may pull. Test them after going through water and dry them by driving slowly while applying light pressure.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 67, NV p. 58, FL p. 80)

prompt: Which headlight setting should you use in fog?
choices: High beams
Parking lights only
Headlights off so they don't reflect
Low beams
explanation: Low beams light the road without bouncing back into your eyes, and they help others see you. Never drive in fog with only parking lights.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 70, FL p. 79, PA p. 46)

prompt: You are driving in fog and can barely see. What can help you stay in your lane?
choices: Follow close behind the taillights ahead
Drive on top of the center line
Watch the brake lights of oncoming cars
Use the right edge line as a guide
explanation: Road edge lines and center lines are useful guides when visibility is poor. Following another car closely leaves you no room to stop.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 79)

prompt: Fog hides most of the clues that tell you how fast you are going. What should you do?
choices: Match the speed of the vehicle behind you so it doesn't hit you
Set cruise control at the posted limit
Check your speedometer often so you don't creep faster
Speed up so you get out of the fog sooner
explanation: Without visual clues it is easy to creep faster than you think. Keep checking your speed and drive slowly enough to stop within the distance you can see.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 46, CA p. 70)

prompt: The fog becomes so thick that you cannot see well enough to drive safely. What should you do?
choices: Stop in your lane, turn on your hazard flashers, and wait it out
Pull completely off the road, turn on your flashers, and wait
Keep going and follow the car ahead closely
Switch to high beams and continue at the same speed
explanation: Stopping in a travel lane in fog invites a rear-end crash. Get fully off the road, preferably into a parking area, and wait for the fog to clear.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 70, PA p. 46)

prompt: Which is a good practice when you must drive in fog?
choices: Increase your following distance and avoid passing
Use only your fog lights instead of headlights
Pass slow vehicles to get clear of the fog
Drive in the left lane to stay away from the shoulder
explanation: In fog, slow down, use low beams, leave extra space ahead and avoid changing lanes or passing unless absolutely necessary.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 70)

prompt: In cold weather, which part of the road often freezes first?
choices: Bridges and overpasses
Sunny stretches of open highway
Busy downtown intersections
Freshly paved roads
explanation: Bridges and overpasses tend to freeze before the rest of the road, so they can be icy even when other pavement is just wet.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 67, NY p. 64, PA p. 45)

prompt: On a cold, wet day, where is ice most likely to remain on the road?
choices: On stretches of road in full, direct sunshine
In lanes with heavy traffic
On roads near the center of town
In spots shaded by trees or buildings
explanation: Shaded areas freeze first and dry out last, so they can hold hidden icy spots after the rest of the road looks clear.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 67, PA p. 45)

prompt: What is "black ice"?
choices: Ice mixed with dirt that is easy to see
Ice that forms only on gravel and dirt roads in winter
A thin, clear ice layer that makes the road look wet
Snow packed down hard by traffic
explanation: Black ice is a thin, nearly invisible coating of ice. Because you can see the dark pavement through it, it looks like a wet road.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 45)

prompt: On a freezing morning, the road ahead looks wet, but the cars in front of you are not throwing up any spray. What could this mean?
choices: The road is drying, so you can speed up
There may be black ice, so ease off and avoid sudden moves
The road has been salted and treated, so it is safe to drive normally
The cars ahead must have new tires
explanation: When a road looks wet but tires are not throwing water, the "water" may actually be ice. Slow down gently without hard braking or sharp steering.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 45)

prompt: When is ice usually the MOST slippery?
choices: On extremely cold, dry days
When it is near freezing and wet on top
When it is covered with a deep layer of fresh snow
Late at night in a well-lit city
explanation: Ice near the freezing point often has a film of water on it, which is even more slippery than ice alone. Be extra careful when rain or sleet falls near freezing.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 45)

prompt: How should you brake, steer and accelerate on snow or ice?
choices: Gently and smoothly
Quickly and firmly to stay in control
The same as on dry pavement if you have snow tires
Only with the parking brake
explanation: Sudden or hard inputs can break traction and cause a skid. Brake early and gently, steer smoothly, and accelerate slowly.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 64, PA p. 45, CA p. 66)

prompt: You are approaching a stop sign on a snow-covered road. What should you do?
choices: Brake at the usual point, but press harder
Shift into neutral and coast up to the sign
Keep your speed until the last moment, then brake firmly
Start braking earlier and more gently than usual
explanation: Stopping takes much more distance on snow and ice. Begin slowing early with steady, gentle pressure so the wheels keep turning.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 64, CA p. 66)

prompt: Your vehicle has four-wheel drive. How does that affect driving on ice?
choices: It lets you drive at normal speed on ice
It makes your stopping distance on ice much shorter
It helps you get moving but not stop or turn on ice
It means you no longer need extra following distance
explanation: Four-wheel and all-wheel drive improve traction for getting going, but they do not prevent skids or shorten braking distance. Slow down like everyone else.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 64, CO p. 19)

prompt: Before driving after a snowfall, what should you clear of snow and ice?
choices: Only a small spot on the windshield in front of you
Only the windshield; the other windows will clear while driving
All windows, mirrors, lights, and the roof and hood
Only the headlights
explanation: You need a full view and your lights must be visible. Snow left on the roof or hood can slide onto your windshield or blow onto drivers behind you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 46, NY p. 64)

prompt: On an icy road, why is it dangerous to brake hard in the middle of a curve?
choices: Your brake lights are hard to see in a curve
The tires can lose grip and start a skid
Brakes do not work while the wheels are turned
It is only a problem in cars with four-wheel drive
explanation: Braking hard while turning on a slippery surface can break traction and cause a skid. Slow down on the straight road before the curve, then drive through it smoothly.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 66, PA p. 44)

prompt: Besides ice and snow, which of these can make the road surface very slick?
choices: Wet leaves
Dry concrete
Fresh, dry asphalt
A dry, freshly swept parking lot
explanation: Wet leaves, oil and standing water can be as slippery as ice. Slow down and avoid them when you safely can.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 63, CA p. 66)

prompt: What most often causes a car to skid on a slippery road?
choices: Driving with low-beam headlights
Driving too slowly on a long, straight stretch of road
Keeping a long following distance
Driving too fast and making sudden moves
explanation: Skids happen when tires lose grip. Excess speed and sudden steering, braking or acceleration are the usual causes, so drive slowly and smoothly.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 66, PA p. 44)

prompt: You are driving up a snowy hill behind another car. What should you do?
choices: Follow closely so you can use its tracks
Pass it so you are not stuck behind it
Brake often to test your traction on the way up
Hang back so you won't have to stop partway up
explanation: Stopping on a snowy upgrade can leave you unable to get moving again. Hang back so you can keep a slow, steady pace to the top.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 45)

prompt: How should you drive in strong winds?
choices: Speed up to spend less time in the wind
Use cruise control to hold a steady speed
Slow down and keep a firm grip on the steering wheel
Loosen your grip a little so the car can drift with the gusts
explanation: Gusts are unpredictable. A lower speed and a firm grip give you more control and time to react when the wind pushes your vehicle.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 69, AZ p. 54)

prompt: On a windy day, you drive from a sheltered stretch of road onto an open bridge. What should you expect?
choices: Calmer winds, since bridges are usually protected from wind
A sudden crosswind that may push you sideways
Your brakes locking up
Better tire grip in the open
explanation: When you leave a protected area for an open space, strong crosswinds can push you toward the side or middle of the road. Be ready to correct your steering.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 54)

prompt: Which vehicles are most affected by strong crosswinds?
choices: Campers, trucks and vehicles pulling trailers
Low, heavy passenger sedans
All vehicles are affected equally by crosswinds
Vehicles with all-wheel drive
explanation: Tall vehicles and vehicles towing trailers catch more wind and are the hardest to control in strong winds. Lightweight vehicles are also affected.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 69, AZ p. 54)

prompt: You come to a road covered by moving water. What should you do?
choices: Drive through slowly in a low gear
Speed up so you make it across
Follow a larger vehicle through
Turn around and find another route
explanation: "Turn Around, Don't Drown." You can't tell how deep or fast the water is, and many flood deaths happen in vehicles.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 56, PA p. 66, NV p. 59)

prompt: About how deep does water on the road need to be to reach the bottom of most passenger cars, risking loss of control or stalling?
choices: About 6 inches
About 18 inches
About 3 feet
Deep enough to reach the door handles
explanation: About six inches of water reaches the bottom of most passenger cars and can cause loss of control or stalling. About two feet of moving water can carry away most vehicles, including SUVs.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 56, AK p. 84)

prompt: A driver says, "My SUV sits high, so it can safely cross a flooded road." Which statement is true?
choices: Two feet of moving water can carry away most SUVs and pickups
An SUV can cross moving water safely if four-wheel drive is on
A tall vehicle is safe as long as the water is below its doors
Only small, light cars can be swept away by floodwater
explanation: Moving water pushes on the whole vehicle and can lift it off the road. Two feet of moving water is enough to sweep away most SUVs and pickups.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 66, TX p. 56, AK p. 84)

prompt: Why is it unsafe to drive onto a flooded road that looks shallow?
choices: Shallow water only affects large trucks
You can't judge its depth, and the road may be washed out
Floodwater always ruins the brakes for good
Water on the road is illegal to drive through in every state
explanation: Water can hide missing pavement, collapsed roadbed, debris and even a missing bridge. Its depth is very hard to judge by looking.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 69, TX p. 56, PA p. 66)

prompt: Your car stalls in rising floodwater. What should you do?
choices: Get out quickly and move to higher ground
Stay inside with the windows up until the water goes down
Keep trying to restart the engine
Push the car back the way you came
explanation: Rising water can lift and carry a car away and trap the people inside. Leave the vehicle quickly and get to higher ground.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 56, PA p. 66)

prompt: Before going down a long, steep hill, what should you do?
choices: Shift into neutral and coast
Shift into the highest gear
Turn off the engine to save fuel
Shift into a lower gear
explanation: A lower gear lets the engine help hold your speed down, so you don't have to rely only on your brakes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 20, CA p. 66, PA p. 45)

prompt: Why should you avoid riding your brakes all the way down a long mountain grade?
choices: It wears out your tires quickly but does not affect your brakes
It drains the battery
Constant braking can overheat the brakes so they fade
It causes the engine to stall
explanation: Brakes produce heat, and long, steady braking can overheat them so they fade. Use a lower gear and brake firmly only when needed.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NV p. 58); AAMVA CDL Manual, Section 2.17

prompt: On a steep downgrade, a driver shifts into neutral to save fuel. Why is this a bad idea?
choices: It is fine as long as the brakes are new
It only matters for manual-transmission cars
Without engine braking, the brakes must do all the work
Neutral gives better control because the wheels roll freely
explanation: Coasting in neutral removes the engine's braking effect, so the vehicle speeds up and the brakes can overheat. Many states also prohibit it.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 50, AL p. 75, GA p. 5, AK p. 79)

prompt: What should you expect when driving through a highway work zone?
choices: Sudden stops, shifting lanes, and workers near traffic
Higher speed limits so traffic clears faster
No changes in traffic if you don't see any workers right away
Signals that apply only to trucks
explanation: Work zones change normal traffic patterns. Slow down, leave extra space, and expect sudden stops and lane changes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 55, TX p. 41, NY p. 49)

prompt: You drive through a work zone at night and see no workers. What should you do?
choices: Treat the zone as closed for the night and use any lane that looks open
Return to your normal speed, since no one is working
Stay alert and obey the signs until the zone ends
Drive between the cones to avoid uneven pavement
explanation: Road work can happen at night, workers may be out of sight, and lane shifts and hazards remain. Follow the signs until you pass the end-of-work-zone sign.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 49, TX p. 42, CA p. 65)

prompt: Cones and arrow panels in a work zone show that your lane is closed ahead. What should you do?
choices: Drive between the cones to save time if no workers are present
Slow down and merge into the open lane when it is safe
Stop in your lane until it reopens
Use the shoulder to get past the closed lane
explanation: Channelizing devices guide you safely around the work area. Slow down, check traffic, and merge into the open lane; never drive through or between the cones.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 55, TX p. 42)

prompt: When are deer and other wild animals most active near roads?
choices: At dawn and dusk
At midday
Between midnight and 3 a.m.
Only during rainstorms
explanation: Animals move the most around sunrise and sunset, which is also when visibility is poor. Be extra alert at those times.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 64, FL p. 79, MT p. 71)

prompt: A deer crosses the road ahead of you. What should you expect?
choices: More deer may follow, so slow down
It is the only one, so you can speed up
It will always stay on the far shoulder
It will freeze and stay in place until you pass
explanation: Deer usually travel in groups. If you see one, slow down and watch for others that may follow.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 64, MT p. 71)

prompt: A small animal suddenly runs in front of your car, and there is oncoming traffic. What should you do?
choices: Swerve into the oncoming lane to miss it
Swerve onto the shoulder at full speed
Speed up to get past before it moves
Brake firmly and stay in your lane
explanation: Swerving can cause a much worse crash with another vehicle, a tree or a rollover. Brake firmly and keep control of your vehicle in your lane.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AK p. 72, FL p. 79, MT p. 71)

prompt: At night on a rural road, how can you spot animals early?
choices: Watch only the center line
Scan the road edges for eyes reflecting your lights
Look only at the road surface directly in front of the hood
Keep your eyes on the taillights ahead
explanation: Animals' eyes often shine in your headlights. Scan both sides of the road, especially near woods, fields and water.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 79)

prompt: Where should your eyes be while you drive?
choices: Scanning far ahead and to the sides
Fixed on the bumper of the car ahead
On the road just in front of your hood
Mostly on your speedometer
explanation: Keep your eyes moving. Look well ahead, check the sides of the road and glance at your mirrors so you can spot problems early.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 45, PA p. 41, CA p. 63)

prompt: How often should you check your mirrors during normal driving?
choices: Only when you are changing lanes or merging onto a highway
Only when backing up
Only when you hear a horn or siren
Regularly, even when you are not changing lanes
explanation: Checking your mirrors frequently keeps you aware of traffic behind and beside you so you are ready if you need to slow, stop or move over.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 45, CA p. 65, PA p. 42)

prompt: A car is approaching a STOP sign on a side road ahead. What should a defensive driver assume?
choices: It will stop, so you don't need to watch it
It must yield, so you should speed up
It might not stop, so be ready to react
Its driver will wave you through
explanation: Defensive drivers expect others to make mistakes. Don't assume a driver will stop or yield; watch them and be ready to slow or stop.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 45, PA p. 42)

prompt: You are on a narrow street with parked cars on your right and steady oncoming traffic on your left. Both are equally close. What should you do?
choices: Drive close to the parked cars to give oncoming traffic room
Drive near the center line to stay away from car doors
Speed up to get through the narrow area quickly
Slow down and steer a middle path between them
explanation: When dangers on both sides are about equal, slow down and split the difference. If one hazard is greater, give it more room.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 40, CA p. 64)

prompt: A small piece of tire tread suddenly appears in your lane, with traffic beside you. What may be the safer choice?
choices: Swerve hard into the next lane to miss it
Slam on the brakes, no matter who is close behind you
Slow down and drive over it rather than swerving
Steer onto the shoulder at full speed
explanation: A common debris crash happens when a driver swerves, loses control and leaves the road. Hitting small debris is often less dangerous than a sudden swerve.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 70)

prompt: Why should you slow down on a road with many potholes?
choices: Potholes only affect large trucks
They can jolt the car and make the tires lose grip
Driving fast lets the tires skip over the holes without damage
Speed has no effect on how potholes affect you
explanation: Potholes can bounce your vehicle and reduce tire grip. Scan ahead, slow down, and steer around them only when it is safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 20, NJ p. 187)

prompt: It starts raining hard during the day. What should you do with your headlights?
choices: Leave them off, since it is daytime
Turn on your high beams to see better through the rain
Turn on your low beams so other drivers can see you
Turn on only your parking lights
explanation: Use low-beam headlights in rain, snow or fog, even in daytime, so others can see you. High beams reflect off the rain and make it harder to see. Some states also require headlights whenever your wipers are on.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 68, AK p. 67, AR p. 63, NV p. 56)

prompt: On a cold, rainy day, the inside of your windows keeps fogging up. What should you do?
choices: Use the defroster, or open a window slightly
Wipe a small spot clear with your hand and keep driving
Turn on your windshield wipers
Drive faster so the air flow clears the glass
explanation: Fog on the inside of the glass blocks your view. Use the defroster or open a window slightly to clear it. Wipers only clear the outside of the windshield.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 75, PA p. 46, FL p. 79)

prompt: You turn off a paved highway onto a gravel road. How should you change your driving?
choices: Keep the same speed, because gravel grips as well as pavement does
Brake harder than usual in turns to stay in control
Speed up slightly so the tires don't sink into the gravel
Slow down; you need more room to stop and can skid more easily
explanation: Gravel and dirt give your tires less traction than pavement. Slow down, because it takes longer to stop and it is easier to skid when turning.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., MT p. 69, NM p. 23, CO p. 20)

prompt: You come up behind a snowplow that is clearing the road. What is the safest choice?
choices: Pass it quickly on the right, where the road is already plowed
Stay well back and do not try to pass it
Follow closely in its cleared path
Flash your lights so the driver pulls over
explanation: Snowplow drivers can see very little behind them, may stop or turn around, and throw salt and snow. Their plow blades can stick out several feet to the side, so stay well back and don't try to pass.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 64, CO p. 14)

prompt: On a long, steep downgrade, you pass a runaway truck ramp. When may you stop your car on the ramp?
choices: When you need to pull over and let your brakes cool
When you need to put on tire chains
Never; it is only for vehicles that cannot stop
When you want to let faster traffic pass
explanation: Runaway truck (escape) ramps are for large vehicles that have lost their brakes. Never stop, park or put on chains on or near a ramp; an out-of-control truck may need it at any moment.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 62, CO p. 23)

prompt: You are planning a long winter drive through a rural area. Which items are most useful to carry in case you get stranded?
choices: Extra motor oil, a spare air filter and a tire gauge
A blanket, warm clothes, a shovel, sand and food
A camping stove to keep the car warm inside
Jumper cables only, since the battery may die
explanation: For winter trips, carry a blanket, warm clothing, food, a shovel and sand, and a flashlight. Never use a fuel-burning stove or heater inside a closed car, because it can cause carbon monoxide poisoning.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., IL p. 88, AK p. 81)

prompt: Your car gets stuck in a snowstorm far from town, and you can't call for help. What is usually the safest choice?
choices: Walk to find help, even if you can't see far
Run the engine nonstop with all windows closed to stay warm
Leave the car and wait at the side of the road
Stay in your car; it is easier for rescuers to find
explanation: If you are stranded in a snowstorm, stay in your vehicle: it gives shelter and is easier for rescuers to find. Run the engine only for short periods, keep the tailpipe clear of snow and open a window slightly.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., IL p. 88, MT p. 70)
